content:
A common claim in Muslim writing about Christianity runs like this. The cross, it says, was a pagan sign long before Jesus (peace be upon him), adored in India, held by the gods of Egypt and carved on Mithraic monuments, and the church took it over to win the pagans of Rome.[1]

The claim is half right, and the half that is wrong weakens the half that is right. Cross shapes are older than Christianity, and the cross did become a public emblem only after Constantine.

This article aims to provide context to that claim, insha'Allah, in six facts drawn from the Church Fathers, the early manuscripts and the historians of the fourth and fifth centuries. Each is graded for how much weight it can carry, and we say plainly which parts of the familiar list cannot be traced to any source.

Clement of Alexandria, writing about 200, told Christians which images they might cut on a seal ring. He allowed a dove, a fish, a ship running before the wind, a lyre and an anchor. The cross is absent from his list.[2]

His contemporary Tertullian of Carthage called believers "little fishes" born in water after the example of their Ichthys, the Greek word for fish whose letters spell "Jesus Christ, Son of God, Saviour".[3] The fish was the sign Christians chose for themselves when they chose a picture.

Strength: firm. Both texts are primary and early. They show what the church used first, and they say nothing about pagan origins either way.

The Torah says that a man hanged on a tree is cursed by God (Deuteronomy 21:23). Paul applies the verse to Jesus in Galatians 3:13, and he calls Christ crucified "a stumbling block to Jews and folly to Gentiles" (1 Corinthians 1:23).[4] A form of execution kept for slaves and rebels was a hard thing to put on a banner.

Pagan critics nevertheless accused Christians of worshipping crosses. Minucius Felix, a Roman Christian of the late second or early third century, answered the charge directly: "Crosses, moreover, we neither worship nor wish for." He turned it back on his accusers, pointing out that their own military standards and trophies had the shape of a cross.[5]

Strength: firm. The early Christian witness is that the cross was a scandal to be explained. That fits poorly with a picture of a church eager to adopt a pagan emblem.

By about 204 Tertullian could describe Christians tracing a sign on the forehead at every coming in and going out, at dressing, bathing, meals and bedtime. He offers no scripture for it and calls it tradition, custom and faith.[6]

In two papyrus copies of the Gospels from about 200, Papyrus 66 and Papyrus 75, scribes wrote the Greek words for "cross" and "crucify" with a tau and a rho joined, the staurogram. Larry Hurtado argues that the joined letters drew a man on a cross, which would make them the earliest Christian picture of the crucifixion; that reading is his argument, and others weigh it differently.[7]

A crucifixion scene in a public church setting appears only around 430, on the cypress doors of Santa Sabina in Rome; small gems and amulets carry a few earlier ones.[8] Strength: firm on the dates, moderate on Hurtado's reading. The gesture is early, the public image is a fifth-century development.

Eusebius of Caesarea says Constantine told him, under oath, that before the battle of 312 he saw a cross of light above the sun with the words "Conquer by this", and that he then had a standard made: a gilded spear with a crossbar, topped by the letters chi and rho, the labarum.[9] Eusebius gives the story on the emperor's word alone, and historians have debated it ever since.

Sozomen, writing in the 440s, adds that Constantine abolished crucifixion as a punishment out of reverence for the cross. The edict itself does not survive, and the earlier notice in Aurelius Victor gives a humane motive and an ambiguous wording.[10]

Strength: moderate. The turn from shame to public emblem is real and dated to Constantine. It is a political and devotional change inside Christianity, and the sources give it no pagan model.

Socrates Scholasticus records that when the temple of Serapis in Alexandria was demolished in 391, stones were found carved with hieroglyphs in the form of a cross. Christians and pagans each claimed them, and converts who could read the signs said the cross meant "life to come". Socrates himself doubted that the Egyptian priests had foreseen Christ.[11]

The sign he describes is most likely the ankh, the Egyptian hieroglyph for life. Coptic Christians did adapt it into the looped cross, the crux ansata, which appears in Egyptian Christian art from about 400, and some scholars argue that the two shapes met by resemblance more than by borrowing.[12]

Strength: firm that the shapes existed, moderate on borrowing. The one clear case of adoption is local to Egypt and comes after the cross was already the Christian sign.

The claims that the cross was the emblem of Agni, "the light of the world", that it was placed in the hands of Siva, Vishnu and Krishna, that Horus holds one, and that a Mithraic crucifix was dug up in Ireland, circulate through nineteenth-century compilations such as Kersey Graves (1875) and T. W. Doane (1882).[13] Those books rarely name an object, a museum or an inscription that a reader can check.

The crucifixion plaques found in Ireland, such as the Rinnegan plaque, are Christian works of the seventh or eighth century.[14] Augustine's remark that "the very thing which is now called the Christian religion existed among the ancients" is also misread when it is quoted for this claim: in Retractations 1.13.3 he means that the true worship of God existed from the beginning and later received the name Christian.[15]

Strength: thin, and to be dropped. A Muslim case loses force when it leans on claims that a Christian reader can show have no source. The Quran asks for proof, and these items have none.

The bottom line

The cross became the sign of Christianity through the church's own history: a scandal in the first century, a private gesture by the third, an imperial emblem under Constantine and a public image by the fifth. Cross shapes existed before Christianity, and in Egypt one was absorbed. The wider claim that the church copied the cross from pagan religion has no source that can bear it.

The Muslim objection rests on firmer ground elsewhere. The Quran says of Jesus that "they did not kill him, nor did they crucify him" (4:157), and the Prophet ﷺ said that the son of Mary will return and break the cross.[16] The disagreement is about what happened to Jesus, and on that question the sources, read fairly, are enough. Allahu alam.

Notes

  1. Common in Muslim polemical writing of the late 1990s and 2000s, drawing on the nineteenth-century compilations named in note 13.
  2. Clement of Alexandria, Paedagogus (The Instructor) 3.11, trans. William Wilson, in Ante-Nicene Fathers, vol. 2.
  3. Tertullian, On Baptism 1, trans. S. Thelwall, in Ante-Nicene Fathers, vol. 3.
  4. Deuteronomy 21:23; Galatians 3:13; 1 Corinthians 1:23 (English Standard Version).
  5. Minucius Felix, Octavius 29, trans. Robert Ernest Wallis, in Ante-Nicene Fathers, vol. 4.
  6. Tertullian, The Chaplet (De Corona) 3 to 4, trans. S. Thelwall, in Ante-Nicene Fathers, vol. 3.
  7. Larry W. Hurtado, The Earliest Christian Artifacts: Manuscripts and Christian Origins (Grand Rapids: Eerdmans, 2006); Larry W. Hurtado, "The Staurogram", Biblical Archaeology Review 39:2 (March/April 2013).
  8. The wooden doors of Santa Sabina, Rome, about 430 to 435; on their date and the crucifixion panel, "The Crucifixion Conundrum and the Santa Sabina Doors", Harvard Theological Review.
  9. Eusebius, Life of Constantine 1.28 to 31, trans. Ernest Cushing Richardson, in Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, second series, vol. 1.
  10. Sozomen, Ecclesiastical History 1.8, in Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, second series, vol. 2; Aurelius Victor, De Caesaribus 41.4; John Granger Cook, Crucifixion in the Mediterranean World (Tübingen: Mohr Siebeck, 2014).
  11. Socrates Scholasticus, Ecclesiastical History 5.17, trans. A. C. Zenos, in Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, second series, vol. 2.
  12. On the crux ansata in Coptic art from about 400, and the debate over borrowing, see the summaries in museum catalogues of Coptic textiles, for example the Victoria and Albert Museum, London.
  13. Kersey Graves, The World's Sixteen Crucified Saviors (Boston, 1875); T. W. Doane, Bible Myths and their Parallels in other Religions (New York, 1882).
  14. The Rinnegan crucifixion plaque, gilt bronze, late seventh or early eighth century, National Museum of Ireland.
  15. Augustine, Retractations 1.13.3, on his earlier work De vera religione.
  16. Quran 4:157 (Saheeh International); Sahih al-Bukhari 2222 and 3448, report of Abu Hurayra.
